scenes.tts: In 1910 a white-eyed male fruit fly turned up in a laboratory full of red-eyed flies. Its crosses gave different answers, depending on which parent was white. Mendel's peas never did this. So why would the parent matter here?
scenes.visual: Two reciprocal crosses of white and red flies, each ending in a question box; a not-equal sign lights between the two answers.
scenes.narration: In 1910 a white-eyed male fruit fly turned up in a laboratory full of red-eyed flies. Its crosses gave different answers, depending on which parent was white. Mendel's peas never did this. So why would the parent matter here?

scenes.tts: The answer is the X chromosome. A female fly is X X. A male fly is X Y. The white gene sits on the X, and the Y carries no copy. So a male is hemizygous. He has one copy, not two. And he gets his only X from his mother.
scenes.caption: The answer is the X chromosome. A female fly is XX. A male fly is XY. The white gene sits on the X, and the Y carries no copy. So a male is hemizygous. He has one copy, not two. And he gets his only X from his mother.
scenes.visual: Female XX and male XY chromosomes with the white gene marked; the Y has an empty slot; an arrow carries the mother's X to the male.
scenes.narration: The answer is the X chromosome. A female fly is XX. A male fly is XY. The white gene sits on the X, and the Y carries no copy. So a male is hemizygous. He has one copy, not two. And he gets his only X from his mother.

scenes.tts: Write X plus for the red allele, and X w for white. Cross a red female, X plus X plus, to a white male, X w Y. Every daughter is X plus X w. Every son is X plus Y. All of them have red eyes. Now cross those flies to each other. The daughters all get X plus from their father, so they are red. The sons get their X from the mother, so half are white. Overall, three red flies to one white. Every white fly is a male.
scenes.caption: Write X+ for the red allele, and Xw for white. Cross a red female, X+X+, to a white male, XwY. Every daughter is X+Xw. Every son is X+Y. All of them have red eyes. Now cross those flies to each other. The daughters all get X+ from their father, so they are red. The sons get their X from the mother, so half are white. Overall, three red flies to one white. Every white fly is a male.
scenes.visual: Cross A: parents and all-red children, then a Punnett square of the intercross with a 3 red to 1 white tally; the white cell is a male.
scenes.narration: Write X+ for the red allele, and Xw for white. Cross a red female, X+X+, to a white male, XwY. Every daughter is X+Xw. Every son is X+Y. All of them have red eyes. Now cross those flies to each other. The daughters all get X+ from their father, so they are red. The sons get their X from the mother, so half are white. Overall, three red flies to one white. Every white fly is a male.

scenes.tts: Now reverse the cross. A white female, X w X w, meets a red male, X plus Y. The daughters are X plus X w, and red. The sons are X w Y, and white. The father's eyes pass to his daughters. The mother's pass to her sons. This is called criss-cross inheritance.
scenes.caption: Now reverse the cross. A white female, XwXw, meets a red male, X+Y. The daughters are X+Xw, and red. The sons are XwY, and white. The father's eyes pass to his daughters. The mother's pass to her sons. This is called criss-cross inheritance.
scenes.visual: Cross B: white mother and red father, red daughters and white sons, arrows crossing from father to daughters and mother to sons.
scenes.narration: Now reverse the cross. A white female, XwXw, meets a red male, X+Y. The daughters are X+Xw, and red. The sons are XwY, and white. The father's eyes pass to his daughters. The mother's pass to her sons. This is called criss-cross inheritance.

scenes.tts: Now cross those F one flies to each other. The mother makes eggs with X plus or X w. The father makes sperm with X w or Y. Each of the four combinations has probability one quarter. That gives one red female, one white female, one red male, and one white male. Among four hundred flies, expect one hundred of each.
scenes.caption: Now cross those F1 flies to each other. The mother makes eggs with X+ or Xw. The father makes sperm with Xw or Y. Each of the four combinations has probability one quarter. That gives one red female, one white female, one red male, and one white male. Among 400 flies, expect 100 of each.
scenes.visual: Punnett square of the Cross B intercross; each cell shows 1/4, then 100.
scenes.narration: Now cross those F1 flies to each other. The mother makes eggs with X+ or Xw. The father makes sperm with Xw or Y. Each of the four combinations has probability one quarter. That gives one red female, one white female, one red male, and one white male. Among 400 flies, expect 100 of each.

scenes.tts: An autosomal gene would give the same first generation in both crosses. These crosses differ, and the difference follows the X. Sons always take the mother's allele. So the gene is on the X. Mendel's segregation still holds. Real broods are noisier than these expectations.
scenes.visual: Autosomal expectation (same F1 twice) versus the real crosses (different F1); the mother's X passes to the son, so the gene is on the X.
scenes.narration: An autosomal gene would give the same first generation in both crosses. These crosses differ, and the difference follows the X. Sons always take the mother's allele. So the gene is on the X. Mendel's segregation still holds. Real broods are noisier than these expectations.
